html:
A substantial fraction of cortical learning occurs offline, during sleep. The broad theory of sleep-dependent memory consolidation and its inter-system coordination (hippocampal replay driving cortical model updating, reward-biased reactivation, systems-level reorganization) is developed in "Offline Learning"; the emphasis here is on the cortical implementation—the specific mechanisms by which sleep places cortical circuits into an offline plasticity regime and how that regime engages the same synaptic machinery described above. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

A safe framing is not that sleep computes a wholly new set of learning rules, but that it places cortical circuits into an offline plasticity regime in which recently active ensembles—especially those associated with salient or rewarded experiences—are reactivated under oscillatory conditions that favor stabilization. In motor cortex, learned ensemble patterns replay during post-learning NREM sleep in rodents, and analogous learned motor patterns replay during human sleep 1. In mouse sensory cortex, selective reactivation of learning-activated cortical ensembles during sleep is not merely correlative but can be causally necessary for later memory expression: disrupting this reactivation impairs subsequent fear-memory retrieval, establishing a direct link between sleep-dependent cortical replay and behavioral consolidation 2. A predictive-processing interpretation is that replay provides a second, value-weighted offline pass through the same cortical credit-assignment machinery described in the preceding subsections: the dendritic voltage/Ca 2+ rules, three-factor gating, and branch-local consolidation mechanisms do not shut down during sleep but are instead driven by internally generated reactivation patterns rather than external sensory input. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

A key candidate mechanism by which offline replay becomes plasticity-relevant is the precise temporal coordination of NREM sleep rhythms. Slow oscillations (SO), spindles, and ripples form a nested temporal hierarchy that is thought to organize windows of excitability and interareal communication during consolidation. In rodents, neocortical dendritic Ca2+ activity is elevated and synchronized during spindle-rich sleep, and cortical pyramidal-cell Ca2+ signals are markedly amplified when spindles occur in SO upstates 3, 4. In humans, the precision of SO–spindle coupling predicts endogenous memory reactivation strength, and reactivation strength predicts consolidation 5. Human intracranial work further shows that, under SO upstate control, spindles set a temporal frame in which ripples occur, while cortical ripples during NREM tend to occur near the down-to-upstate transition, often with spindles, and are associated with unit co-firing in an STDP-relevant range 6, 7, 8. Thus, the most defensible claim is that coupled sleep rhythms provide a temporal scaffold that may bias replay toward the biophysical conditions favorable for cortical plasticity and consolidation.

Sleep-dependent consolidation of at least some forms of cortical plasticity engages late-phase biochemical machinery overlapping with that described in the three-factor and synaptic-tagging literatures. In visual cortex, sleep consolidates ocular-dominance plasticity through intracortical NMDAR- and PKA-dependent potentiation-related processes, and blocking mTOR-dependent protein synthesis during sleep abolishes consolidation while reducing sleep-dependent translation of plasticity-related mRNAs such as ARC and BDNF 9, 10. These findings provide one of the clearest cortical links between offline activity and protein-synthesis-dependent stabilization: sleep is not merely permissive ‘time off’ from sensory processing, but an active state in which waking-induced plasticity can be further consolidated. A reasonable STC-like interpretation is that waking experience sets synapse-specific plasticity states or tags, and subsequent sleep provides molecular conditions favorable for PRP capture and lasting stabilization, although this tag-capture mechanism has not yet been demonstrated directly in cortex during sleep 11. More broadly, sleep can preferentially reactivate and strengthen salient or rewarded traces, suggesting that neuromodulatory signals during encoding may bias which memories are later replayed and consolidated, though the exact role of neuromodulators during sleep itself remains unsettled 12, 13.
